learnerStatement: Simulated learner. This review finds problems; it is not evidence that anyone learned.
learnerBoundary: Everyday numeracy, simple charts, comparing numbers and familiar household objects; no domain-specific theory assumed.

observations.prediction: Selected It raises it and locked the chance of total seven after seeing first die three.
observations.exploration: For total seven, first die three, one and six each left the chance at one sixth, matching six of thirty-six before the clue. Switched to total eight: first die six raised chance from five of thirty-six to one sixth; first die one reduced it to zero of six.
observations.reveal: The reveal corrected the answer to unchanged and explained every row has exactly one completion to seven. It accurately quoted the original first-die-three case and the last impossible eight case, then distinguished independence for seven from dependence for eight.
observations.visual: Inspected the inline dark 1257 by 936 screenshot with first die three and total seven. A six by six outcome grid dimmed all but the selected row; one bright 3+4 cell remained a success. Before and after fractions were readable below.
observations.isolation: No-history evaluation preview banner present. Visible trust count ignored.
observations.reference: Own CUA tab 543884179 snapshots and inspected inline screenshot; no screenshot file saved.

prediction.reason: The question tests whether learning part of an outcome must alter the event probability.
prediction.evidence: Selected an increase after the first-die clue.

interaction.reason: Multiple clues and a contrasting target isolate event-specific independence.
interaction.evidence: Seven remains one sixth; eight can become one sixth or impossible.

payoff.reason: The reveal explains the structural row count and accurately references observed cases.
payoff.evidence: One successful completion exists in every row for seven but not eight.

clarity.reason: The grid shows numerator and denominator changing together.
clarity.evidence: The selected six-cell row retains one bright success for seven.

transfer.reason: The formal independence idea is named without a distinct new application.
transfer.evidence: The contrast remains within the same two dice setup.

accessibility.evidence: Keyboard, focus, contrast audit, phone, zoom/reflow and motion unknown.

surprise.reason: Knowing a die value can leave one sum's chance unchanged but alter another.
surprise.evidence: Seven and eight respond differently to the same first-die clue.

visualExplanation.reason: The row restriction and highlighted success cells explain both invariance and failure.
visualExplanation.evidence: The impossible eight row contains no successful completion.

playfulness.reason: Clue and total controls invite testing a counterexample.
playfulness.evidence: Several die values and two targets can be compared.

practicalValue.reason: It gives a concrete definition of event independence.
practicalValue.evidence: A clue matters only if it changes the relevant event's probability.

depth.reason: The lesson prevents overgeneralizing independence from a single case.
depth.evidence: Total eight provides an explicit contrasting event.

complexity.reason: Simple dice support a subtle distinction between conditional probability and event independence.
complexity.conceptualDemand: Moderate: compare conditional and unconditional ratios.
complexity.interfaceBurden: Low: first-die choices and two total targets.
complexity.conceptualChallenge: Information can reduce the sample space without changing a particular event's fraction.
complexity.prerequisiteNovelty: Conditional probability and independence are introduced.
complexity.notationRepresentationBurden: Moderate: outcome grid and before-after fractions.

whyCool: A clue can shrink the possibilities dramatically while preserving one event's exact probability.
caveat: The outcomes assume fair independent dice, and only two sum targets are available.
missingEvidence: No fresh target event or different probability setup was tested.
